shorts.title: Why the Western Front Froze Into Trenches
shorts.description: Why did World War I’s Western Front turn into a trench line? In under a minute: the Marne, the Race to the Sea, trench warfare, 1918, and the armistice.

scenes.name: The 1914 rush
scenes.script: Germany’s 1914 plan drove through Belgium toward France. But French and British forces stopped the advance at the First Battle of the Marne.
scenes.caption: 1914: the advance is stopped

scenes.name: Race to the Sea
scenes.script: Both sides then tried to outflank each other northward. By late 1914, trenches stretched from the North Sea toward Switzerland.
scenes.caption: A front becomes a trench system

scenes.name: Why attacks stalled
scenes.script: Machine guns, artillery, barbed wire, and deep defenses made crossing open ground brutally expensive. Huge offensives often gained little ground.
scenes.caption: Firepower favored defense

scenes.name: 1918 breaks the stalemate
scenes.script: Germany’s spring offensives advanced in 1918, but they failed to force a decision. Allied counterattacks, reinforced by growing American forces, pushed the front back.
scenes.caption: 1918: advance, then reversal

scenes.name: How it ended
scenes.script: The Allied Hundred Days offensive kept pressure on Germany. With its army exhausted and allies collapsing, Germany accepted the armistice on November 11, 1918.
scenes.caption: Armistice · November 11, 1918

sources: Imperial War Museums — First World War

shorts.title: Why the Eastern Front Kept Moving
shorts.description: The Eastern Front of World War I was far more mobile than the trench-bound west. Here’s why Russia, Germany, and Austria-Hungary fought across enormous distances.

scenes.name: A gigantic front
scenes.script: In the east, armies fought across a far larger area than in France and Belgium. That made one continuous trench wall much harder to maintain.
scenes.caption: A front stretching hundreds of miles

scenes.name: Tannenberg
scenes.script: Russia invaded East Prussia in 1914. Germany surrounded and defeated one Russian army at Tannenberg, while fighting continued farther south against Austria-Hungary.
scenes.caption: 1914: Tannenberg

scenes.name: The Great Retreat
scenes.script: In 1915, the Central Powers broke through at Gorlice–Tarnów. Russian armies retreated far east, giving up large territories in Poland and beyond.
scenes.caption: 1915: the front moves east

scenes.name: Russia strikes back
scenes.script: The 1916 Brusilov Offensive smashed much of Austria-Hungary’s front and forced Germany to send help east, but Russia paid heavily too.
scenes.caption: 1916: Brusilov Offensive

scenes.name: Russia leaves the war
scenes.script: Revolution shattered the Russian war effort in 1917. The Bolshevik government signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918, ending Russia’s participation.
scenes.caption: 1918: Russia exits World War I

sources: Imperial War Museums — First World War

shorts.title: Pearl Harbor in Under a Minute: Why Japan Attacked
shorts.description: What caused Pearl Harbor, what happened on December 7, 1941, and why the attack did not knock the United States out of the Pacific War.

scenes.name: Why tensions exploded
scenes.script: Japan had been expanding through China and Southeast Asia. In 1941, after Japan moved into southern Indochina, the United States froze Japanese assets and effectively cut off access to American oil.
scenes.caption: 1941: oil and empire collide

scenes.name: The strike route
scenes.script: Japan chose a surprise carrier strike to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet while Japanese forces moved toward resource-rich territories farther south.
scenes.caption: A surprise strike across the Pacific

scenes.name: December 7, 1941
scenes.script: On the morning of December 7, Japanese aircraft hit Pearl Harbor. In less than two hours, more than 2,400 Americans were killed and numerous ships and aircraft were destroyed or damaged.
scenes.caption: Pearl Harbor is attacked

scenes.name: What Japan missed
scenes.script: No American aircraft carriers were in Pearl Harbor that morning. Japan also left major fuel storage and repair facilities intact, helping the U.S. recover faster than Japan hoped.
scenes.caption: The fleet was hurt—not eliminated

scenes.name: America enters the war
scenes.script: The United States declared war on Japan the next day. Germany and Italy declared war on the United States days later, turning America fully into a global war.
scenes.caption: December 8: U.S. declares war

sources: The National WWII Museum — Pearl Harbor Attack, December 7, 1941
The National WWII Museum — The Path to Pearl Harbor

shorts.title: Midway: The Battle That Broke Japan’s Carrier Force
shorts.description: Six months after Pearl Harbor, the Battle of Midway changed the balance in the Pacific. Here’s the codebreaking, ambush, and four-carrier loss in under a minute.

scenes.name: Japan’s plan
scenes.script: In June 1942, Japan aimed to seize Midway and draw the U.S. Pacific Fleet into a battle where it could be destroyed.
scenes.caption: Midway was the bait

scenes.name: Codebreakers changed the odds
scenes.script: American codebreakers had identified Midway as the target. Admiral Nimitz positioned U.S. carriers northeast of the atoll to surprise the Japanese fleet.
scenes.caption: The ambush is set

scenes.name: June 4
scenes.script: On June 4, Japanese aircraft attacked Midway. While Japanese decks were busy rearming and refueling, American carrier aircraft found the fleet.
scenes.caption: Both sides launch aircraft

scenes.name: Four carriers lost
scenes.script: U.S. dive bombers struck three Japanese carriers within minutes; a fourth was hit later. Japan lost Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and Hiryu.
scenes.caption: Four Japanese fleet carriers lost

scenes.name: Why Midway mattered
scenes.script: Midway did not end the Pacific War, but it destroyed much of Japan’s elite carrier striking force and shifted the strategic initiative toward the United States.
scenes.caption: A major strategic turning point

sources: The National WWII Museum — Battle of Midway

shorts.title: D-Day in 45 Seconds: How Normandy Was Breached
shorts.description: How the Allies crossed the English Channel on June 6, 1944: airborne troops, five beaches, the Normandy foothold, and the opening of the Western Front.

scenes.name: Operation Overlord
scenes.script: On June 6, 1944, Allied forces launched Operation Overlord—the invasion of Nazi-occupied France across the English Channel.
scenes.caption: June 6, 1944

scenes.name: Airborne first
scenes.script: Before the beach landings, American and British airborne troops dropped behind German defenses to seize roads, bridges, and key positions.
scenes.caption: Paratroopers land behind the coast

scenes.name: Five beaches
scenes.script: The seaborne assault hit five beaches: Utah and Omaha for the Americans, Gold and Sword for the British, and Juno for the Canadians.
scenes.caption: Utah · Omaha · Gold · Juno · Sword

scenes.name: A foothold, not a finish
scenes.script: The Allies did not achieve every first-day objective, and fighting was especially costly at Omaha. But they secured beachheads that Germany could not throw back into the sea.
scenes.caption: The beachhead survives

scenes.name: Why D-Day mattered
scenes.script: The Normandy lodgment opened the Western Front in Europe. Over the following weeks, Allied armies built up strength and began the campaign to liberate France.
scenes.caption: The liberation of Western Europe begins

sources: U.S. National Archives — Records Relating to D-Day

shorts.title: Why the American Revolution Started
shorts.description: Taxes were only part of it. In under a minute: imperial debt, representation, Boston, Lexington and Concord, independence, France, and Yorktown.

scenes.name: After the Seven Years’ War
scenes.script: After the Seven Years’ War, Britain faced huge debts and tried to raise more revenue from its American colonies. New taxes and tighter imperial control triggered resistance.
scenes.caption: Britain wants revenue

scenes.name: No taxation without representation
scenes.script: Many colonists argued Parliament was taxing them without their consent. The Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Boston Massacre, and Tea Party deepened the crisis.
scenes.caption: Resistance grows

scenes.name: War begins
scenes.script: In April 1775, fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord. The conflict quickly grew from a political crisis into an armed rebellion.
scenes.caption: April 1775: Lexington & Concord

scenes.name: Independence and France
scenes.script: The colonies declared independence in July 1776. After the American victory at Saratoga, France entered the war as an American ally in 1778.
scenes.caption: France changes the balance

scenes.name: Yorktown and peace
scenes.script: British forces surrendered at Yorktown in 1781 after American and French forces trapped Cornwallis. The Treaty of Paris in 1783 formally recognized U.S. independence.
scenes.caption: 1783: independence recognized

sources: U.S. National Park Service — American Revolution resources
U.S. National Archives — Declaration of Independence

shorts.title: French Revolution in Under a Minute
shorts.description: Debt, food prices, unequal taxation, the Estates-General, Bastille, republic, Terror, and Napoleon—France’s revolution in under a minute.

scenes.name: France is in crisis
scenes.script: By 1789, France had heavy state debt, an unfair tax system, and a severe economic crisis. Rising bread prices made anger even worse.
scenes.caption: 1789: debt + inequality + hunger

scenes.name: The Third Estate breaks away
scenes.script: Louis XVI called the Estates-General. Representatives of the Third Estate declared themselves the National Assembly and claimed the right to write a constitution.
scenes.caption: The National Assembly forms

scenes.name: The Bastille
scenes.script: On July 14, 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille. The prison held few inmates, but its fall became a powerful symbol of royal authority collapsing.
scenes.caption: July 14: the Bastille falls

scenes.name: Monarchy to republic
scenes.script: Revolutionary governments abolished feudal privileges and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man. In 1792 France became a republic; Louis XVI was executed in 1793.
scenes.caption: The monarchy falls

scenes.name: Terror, then Napoleon
scenes.script: The revolution radicalized into the Reign of Terror, then shifted to the Directory. In 1799, Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in a coup, ending this phase of the revolution.
scenes.caption: 1799: Napoleon takes power

shorts.title: Waterloo: How Napoleon Lost His Final Battle
shorts.description: Napoleon’s Hundred Days ended at Waterloo. Here’s Ligny, Wellington, Blücher, the Prussian arrival, and the final collapse in under a minute.

scenes.name: Napoleon returns
scenes.script: Napoleon escaped exile on Elba in 1815 and returned to power. European states immediately formed a new coalition to remove him.
scenes.caption: The Hundred Days begin

scenes.name: Split the coalition
scenes.script: Napoleon moved into Belgium hoping to defeat Wellington’s Anglo-Allied army and Blücher’s Prussians before they could fully unite.
scenes.caption: Defeat them separately

scenes.name: Ligny and Quatre Bras
scenes.script: On June 16, Napoleon defeated the Prussians at Ligny, but they were not destroyed. Nearby, French forces failed to decisively dislodge Wellington at Quatre Bras.
scenes.caption: June 16: victory—but not enough

scenes.name: Waterloo
scenes.script: On June 18, Napoleon attacked Wellington at Waterloo. Late in the day, Blücher’s Prussians arrived on the French flank, while Wellington’s line still held.
scenes.caption: The Prussians arrive

scenes.name: The final collapse
scenes.script: A final French attack failed, and Napoleon’s army broke. He abdicated again and was sent to Saint Helena. Waterloo ended his rule for good.
scenes.caption: June 18, 1815: Napoleon defeated

shorts.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: 13 Days Near Nuclear War
shorts.description: In October 1962, U.S. and Soviet leaders came dangerously close to nuclear war over missiles in Cuba. Here’s how the crisis began and ended.

scenes.name: Missiles in Cuba
scenes.script: After the failed Bay of Pigs invasion, the Soviet Union secretly placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, partly to deter another U.S. invasion.
scenes.caption: Soviet missiles arrive in Cuba

scenes.name: The U-2 photographs
scenes.script: On October 14, a U.S. U-2 photographed missile sites in Cuba. President Kennedy was briefed on October 16, beginning the crisis inside the White House.
scenes.caption: U-2 photos reveal the sites

scenes.name: The quarantine
scenes.script: Kennedy chose a naval quarantine rather than an immediate air strike. U.S. ships moved to block additional offensive weapons from reaching Cuba.
scenes.caption: A naval ring around Cuba

scenes.name: October 27: the danger peaks
scenes.script: Tension peaked on October 27: a U-2 was shot down over Cuba while U.S. and Soviet leaders exchanged messages and searched for a way out.
scenes.caption: One mistake could trigger war

scenes.name: The deal
scenes.script: Khrushchev agreed to remove Soviet missiles from Cuba. The United States publicly pledged not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
scenes.caption: The missiles are withdrawn

sources: U.S. Department of State Office of the Historian — Cuban Missile Crisis

shorts.title: Why the Berlin Wall Fell
shorts.description: Why the Berlin Wall was built in 1961, how it divided a city, and why a confused announcement on November 9, 1989 helped bring it down.

scenes.name: Why the wall went up
scenes.script: After World War II, Germany and Berlin were divided. By 1961, East Germany had lost large numbers of people through West Berlin, creating a political and economic crisis.
scenes.caption: Berlin was a Cold War escape route

scenes.name: August 13, 1961
scenes.script: On August 13, East German authorities sealed the border. Barbed wire quickly became concrete walls, guard towers, and a fortified barrier through Berlin.
scenes.caption: The border is sealed

scenes.name: A divided city
scenes.script: The wall divided streets, workplaces, and families. People still tried to escape, while U.S. and Soviet tanks even faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie in 1961.
scenes.caption: Berlin becomes a Cold War symbol

scenes.name: 1989 pressure builds
scenes.script: By 1989, reforms in the Soviet bloc, mass protests in East Germany, and new escape routes through neighboring countries put enormous pressure on the regime.
scenes.caption: The system starts to crack

scenes.name: November 9, 1989
scenes.script: On November 9, a confused announcement about new travel rules sent crowds to border crossings. Guards opened the gates, and Berliners began tearing the wall down. Germany reunified in 1990.
scenes.caption: The gates open

sources: U.S. Department of State Office of the Historian — Berlin Wall
